latest_nl_proof:
Let p>5 be prime with p ≡ 7 (mod 8), and let I(k) be the least positive inverse of k modulo p.

First note that I is an involution on {1,...,p-1}: if a·I(a) ≡ 1 (mod p), then I(a)·a ≡ 1 (mod p), so by uniqueness of the inverse in {1,...,p-1} we have I(I(a))=a.

Define
T := { t in {1,...,p-2} : t + I(t) < p-2 }.
I claim that |S|=|T|.

Indeed, define Phi:{1,...,p-2} -> {1,...,p-2} by
Phi(t)=I(t+1)-1.
Because I is a bijection of {1,...,p-1} and I(1)=1, Phi is a bijection from {1,...,p-2} onto itself.

Fix t in {1,...,p-2}, and set k=Phi(t)=I(t+1)-1. Then k+1=I(t+1), hence (using that I is an involution) I(k+1)=t+1.
Now put y:=p-1-I(t). Since t<=p-2, we have I(t) != p-1, so y lies in {1,...,p-2}. Also, modulo p,
k = I(t+1)-1 ≡ (t+1)^(-1)-1 = -t(t+1)^(-1),
and
y = p-1-I(t) ≡ -1-t^(-1) = -(t+1)t^(-1).
Therefore
k y ≡ [-t(t+1)^(-1)]·[-(t+1)t^(-1)] ≡ 1 (mod p).
By uniqueness of the inverse, y=I(k). Thus
I(k)=p-1-I(t).
Consequently,
k in S
iff I(k+1) < I(k)
iff t+1 < p-1-I(t)
iff t+I(t) < p-2.
Since Phi is a bijection, this proves |S|=|T|.

So it remains to bound |T|.

Let
A := { u in {1,...,p-1} : u+I(u) < p }.
For every u in {1,...,p-1}, we have I(p-u)=p-I(u), hence
(p-u)+I(p-u) = (p-u)+(p-I(u)) = 2p-(u+I(u)).
Thus, in the pair {u,p-u}, one element has sum < p exactly when the other has sum > p. To use this, we must rule out equality u+I(u)=p.

If u+I(u)=p, then multiplying by u gives
u^2 + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p),
so u^2 ≡ -1 (mod p).
But p ≡ 7 (mod 8), hence p ≡ 3 (mod 4), so (p-1)/2 is odd. If u^2 ≡ -1 (mod p), then by Fermat's little theorem,
1 ≡ u^(p-1) = (u^2)^((p-1)/2) ≡ (-1)^((p-1)/2) = -1 (mod p),
a contradiction. So u+I(u) != p for every u.

Therefore, among each pair {u,p-u}, exactly one element belongs to A. There are (p-1)/2 such pairs, so
|A| = (p-1)/2.
Also p-1 is not in A, because (p-1)+I(p-1)=2p-2>p. Hence
|{u in {1,...,p-2}: u+I(u)<p}| = (p-1)/2.

Now T is obtained from this set by removing those u with u+I(u)=p-1 or u+I(u)=p-2.

1) If u+I(u)=p-2, then multiplying by u gives
u^2 + 2u + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p),
so (u+1)^2 ≡ 0 (mod p). Hence u ≡ -1 (mod p), i.e. u=p-1, impossible since u in {1,...,p-2}. So there are no such u.

2) If u+I(u)=p-1, then multiplying by u gives
u^2 + u + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p).
This is a quadratic congruence, so it has at most 2 solutions modulo p.

Therefore
|T| >= (p-1)/2 - 2 = (p-5)/2.
Since p ≡ 7 (mod 8), write p=8m+7. Then
floor(p/4)=2m+1=(p-3)/4,
and
(p-5)/2 - (p-3)/4 = (p-7)/4 = 2m >= 0.
So
|S| = |T| >= (p-5)/2 >= floor(p/4).
This is exactly the desired inequality.
role_in_parent: Covers the final missing residue class modulo 8, completing the repaired case split.
statement_nl: Let p be a prime number with p > 5 and p ≡ 7 (mod 8). For each k in {1,2,...,p-1}, let I(k) be the unique integer in {1,2,...,p-1} such that k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p), and define S = { k in {1,2,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) }. Then |S| >= floor(p/4).

domain_restrictions: p is a prime integer with p > 5 and p ≡ 7 (mod 8) (hence p is odd)
k ranges over integers 1 ≤ k ≤ p-1 when defining I(k); when forming S, k ranges over 1 ≤ k ≤ p-2 so that k+1 ≤ p-1
I(k) is the unique representative in the integer set {1,...,p-1} satisfying k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p)
All comparisons I(k+1) < I(k) are ordinary integer comparisons between these chosen representatives
floor(p/4) denotes the integer floor of p/4; |S| denotes cardinality (a nonnegative integer)
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every prime p > 5 with p ≡ 7 (mod 8), define I: {1,...,p-1} → {1,...,p-1} by letting I(k) be the unique integer in {1,...,p-1} with k·I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p). Let S = { k ∈ {1,...,p-2} | I(k+1) < I(k) }. Then the cardinality of S satisfies |S| ≥ floor(p/4).
quantifier_order: for all p (integer prime) such that p > 5 and p ≡ 7 (mod 8)
define I by: for each k ∈ {1,...,p-1} there exists a unique I(k) ∈ {1,...,p-1} with k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p)

variables.domain: primes p with p > 5 and p ≡ 7 (mod 8)
variables.name: p
variables.role: parameter (quantified: arbitrary prime satisfying the congruence and bound)

variables.domain: for definitions: k ∈ {1,2,...,p-1}; for S: k ∈ {1,2,...,p-2}
variables.name: k
variables.role: index variable ranging over residues modulo p (representatives 1..p-1) used to define inverses and S

variables.name: I
variables.role: maps k to its multiplicative inverse modulo p chosen as the unique representative in {1,...,p-1}

variables.name: S
variables.role: S = { k ∈ {1,...,p-2} | I(k+1) < I(k) } whose cardinality is compared to floor(p/4)

witness_dependencies: I(k) depends on both k and the modulus p (I = inverse modulo p, chosen in 1..p-1)
S depends on the entire function I (hence on p) since membership k ∈ S is decided by values I(k), I(k+1)
The uniqueness existential for I(k) uses gcd(k,p)=1 which holds because p is prime and 1 ≤ k ≤ p-1
